finding: Optimization techniques reduce memory through different mechanisms.
evidence: Quantization reduces bytes per value, sparsity removes zero weights but adds metadata, and model parallelism partitions parameters across devices.
interpretation: They are not interchangeable; each solves a different memory constraint.

finding: The highest analytical reduction came from int4 quantization.
evidence: int4 quantization ranked first with 80.28% average estimated total-memory reduction.
interpretation: Low-bit quantization is highly memory-efficient analytically, but needs runtime validation.

finding: fp16 remains the most defensible measured optimization result.
evidence: fp16 precision gave 46.29% average estimated total-memory reduction and was based on measured fp32/fp16 runs.
interpretation: This should be presented as the strongest measured optimization evidence.

finding: Model parallelism becomes competitive when more devices or fp16 are used.
evidence: fp32 4-device model parallelism gave 62.03% average reduction, while fp16 4-device model parallelism gave 77.30%.
interpretation: Model parallelism is useful for per-device memory reduction but adds distributed-system complexity.

finding: High sparsity can compete with model parallelism analytically.
evidence: 90% unstructured sparsity gave 74.06% average estimated total-memory reduction.
interpretation: Sparse storage can be effective, but only after index metadata overhead is overcome.

finding: Measured and analytical results must be clearly separated.
evidence: int8/int4 quantization, sparsity, and model parallelism were not measured as runtime executions.
interpretation: This keeps the project honest and defensible.
